name: Achievement Scholarship for Refugees and Immigrants of Wake County
description: The Achievement Scholarship for Refugees and Immigrants in Wake County provides financial support for refugee and immigrant high school graduates to continue their education at a post-secondary institution. Administered by the Triangle Community Foundation in North Carolina, the scholarship awards up to $16,000 per recipient distributed annually over four years. Students must maintain a minimum 2.5 GPA and submit semester reports to continue receiving funding. Payments can be applied toward any need listed under the school's total cost of attendance, including tuition, fees, books, housing, and transportation. The program was established to help refugee and immigrant youth in the Raleigh-Durham area overcome financial barriers to higher education and build a pathway to meaningful employment.
eligibility: Graduating high school seniors who are refugees or immigrants residing in Wake County, North Carolina; must be accepted to or enrolled in a post-secondary institution; must maintain a 2.5 GPA and submit semester progress reports to continue receiving funding
amount: Up to $16,000 total — distributed annually over 4 years (approximately $4,000 per year)
applicationProcess: Applications are submitted through the Triangle Community Foundation's scholarship portal. Applicants must be graduating high school seniors who are refugees or immigrants living in Wake County, NC. Required materials typically include a personal essay, academic transcripts, proof of Wake County residency, and at least one letter of recommendation. Application deadlines vary by year — check the Triangle Community Foundation website for current cycle dates. Recipients are selected by a review committee based on academic achievement, financial need, and demonstrated commitment to education.
documentsRequired: High school transcripts; proof of Wake County residency; personal essay; letter(s) of recommendation; proof of refugee or immigrant status (immigration documents, I-94, asylum approval, or similar); acceptance letter from post-secondary institution

name: Global Impact Initiative — CDL Training Program for Refugees
description: The Global Impact Initiative (Gii) offers a fully funded Commercial Driver's License (CDL) training program designed specifically for refugees resettled in the United States. The program covers the full cost of CDL training, including classroom instruction, behind-the-wheel practice, and licensing exam fees. CDL holders can earn competitive wages in the trucking and logistics industry, making this one of the fastest pathways to economic self-sufficiency for newly arrived refugees. The program is based in Austin, Texas, and was launched in response to the growing need for accessible vocational training among refugee communities. Gii also provides wraparound support including job placement assistance, mentorship, and connections to employers actively hiring CDL-certified drivers.
eligibility: Refugees resettled in the United States; must have legal work authorization; must meet state requirements for CDL eligibility including minimum age (typically 21 for interstate commercial driving); basic English proficiency recommended; no prior driving experience required
amount: Fully funded — all training costs, materials, and licensing fees covered at no cost to the participant
applicationProcess: Apply through the Global Impact Initiative website at globalimpactinitiative.com. Applicants complete an intake form indicating their refugee status, work authorization, and interest in CDL training. Gii staff conduct a screening to determine eligibility and readiness. Accepted participants are enrolled in CDL training sessions and provided with scheduling, transportation support, and mentoring throughout the program. Space is limited and enrollment is on a rolling basis.
geographicScope: Austin, Texas — primary location; program may expand to additional cities based on funding
documentsRequired: Proof of refugee status (I-94, asylum approval, or resettlement documentation); valid work authorization (EAD card or equivalent); state-issued ID or driver's permit; Social Security card

name: Oregon Immigrant & Refugee Student Success Plan Grants (2026–2028)
description: The Oregon Department of Education awards Immigrant/Refugee Student Success Plan grants to school districts, early learning centers, education service districts, post-secondary institutions, and community organizations across Oregon. The 2026–2028 grant cycle evaluated over 80 eligible applications and awarded 13 grantees a combined total of more than $3 million. These grants fund programs that directly support immigrant and refugee students through culturally responsive education, family engagement, academic tutoring, language development, college preparation, and wraparound services. The programs benefit immigrant and refugee K-12 students and their families by providing resources that address linguistic, cultural, and socioeconomic barriers to academic success. Students and families can access funded services through their local school districts and partner organizations at no cost.
eligibility: Immigrant and refugee students in Oregon K-12 schools and their families; services delivered through funded school districts, early learning centers, and community organizations; no individual application required — students access services through participating schools and organizations
amount: Over $3,013,000 total across 13 grantees for the 2026–2028 cycle — services provided free to immigrant and refugee students and families
applicationProcess: Individual students and families do not need to apply — services are delivered through funded school districts and partner organizations. Families can contact their local school district or the Oregon Department of Education to find funded programs in their area. Funded organizations offer academic tutoring, language support, family engagement programs, college preparation, and cultural navigation services for immigrant and refugee students.
geographicScope: Oregon — statewide across 13 funded school districts, education service districts, and community organizations
documentsRequired: None for students and families — services are provided through schools and community partners without individual application requirements

name: Illinois FY2026 ESL Expansion for Asylees, Refugees & Migrants
description: The Illinois Community College Board allocated $750,000 in state funding to expand English as a Second Language (ESL) services for adult education providers working with asylees, refugees, and migrants across Illinois. This FY2025–2026 grant program funds community colleges and adult education providers to increase their capacity to serve newly arrived immigrants and refugees who need English language instruction to integrate into their communities, find employment, and access essential services. Funded providers offer free ESL classes at various proficiency levels, from beginning literacy to advanced academic English. The expansion was created in response to the increased arrival of asylum seekers and migrants in Illinois and addresses the critical gap between demand for English language services and available classroom capacity.
eligibility: Adult asylees, refugees, and migrants residing in Illinois who need English language instruction; no immigration status documentation required to enroll in ESL classes at funded providers; classes are free and open to adults of all English proficiency levels
amount: Free ESL classes — $750,000 in total state funding distributed to adult education providers; no cost to individual participants
applicationProcess: Individual students do not need to apply to the ICCB grant. Instead, contact your local community college or adult education provider in Illinois to enroll in free ESL classes. Many providers offer walk-in registration, placement testing, and flexible scheduling including evening and weekend classes. To find a provider near you, visit the ICCB website or contact your local community college's adult education department.
geographicScope: Illinois — statewide, services delivered through community colleges and adult education providers across the state
documentsRequired: Minimal or none — most ESL programs require only proof of age (18+) and Illinois residency; no immigration documentation required to enroll; some programs may request a photo ID for registration purposes

name: English for New Bostonians — Free ESL Network for Immigrants
description: English for New Bostonians (ENB) is a publicly and privately funded initiative that coordinates and supports a network of free and low-cost English language programs for adult immigrants in the greater Boston area. ENB provides grants to community-based organizations, faith-based groups, libraries, and other providers to deliver English classes tailored to immigrant communities. The network includes programs at all levels from basic literacy to advanced English, with specialized tracks for workplace English, civic engagement, and digital literacy. ENB-funded programs serve thousands of adult immigrants annually and are designed to be accessible, with classes offered in community settings, flexible scheduling, and no cost to participants. ENB also provides teacher training, curriculum development, and program quality support to its network of providers, ensuring consistent and effective instruction across all sites.
eligibility: Adult immigrants and refugees residing in the greater Boston area; no immigration status requirement — open to all immigrants regardless of documentation; free or low-cost classes available at various community locations; all English proficiency levels welcome from beginner to advanced
amount: Free or low-cost ESL classes — no charge to individual participants; programs funded through public and private grants
applicationProcess: Visit the English for New Bostonians website at englishfornewbostonians.org to find a list of funded ESL programs in the greater Boston area. Contact programs directly to register. Most programs offer walk-in registration or phone enrollment. A brief placement assessment determines your English level and the best class for you. Classes are held at community centers, libraries, churches, and other accessible locations throughout Boston and surrounding communities.
geographicScope: Greater Boston area, Massachusetts — network of providers across Boston, Cambridge, Somerville, and surrounding communities
documentsRequired: Minimal — most programs require only a photo ID for registration; no Social Security number or immigration documents required; some programs may ask for proof of Boston-area residency
